alignment.note: Greek uses paratactic καί + finite verb (παραλαμβάνει), and the Vulgate mirrors this with Et + assumit; the Peshitta fuses the conjunction with the verb in a single form ܘܕܒܪ ('and he took'), a normal Syriac waw-prefixed construction.
παραλαμβάνει / assumit, the present-tense 'takes/takes along'; note the Greek and Latin retain the historic present whereas the Syriac ܕܒܪ is a perfect.

Greek places μετ᾽ αὐτοῦ ('with him') after the list of names, and Latin secum likewise follows; the Peshitta ܥܡܗ is placed immediately after the verb, before the names, reflecting a typical Syriac preference for early prepositional positioning.
Πέτρον / ܠܟܐܦܐ / Petrum; the Syriac employs the native Aramaic name ܟܐܦܐ ('Kepha', rock) rather than transliterating the Greek Πέτρος, preserving the original Semitic designation.
Ἰάκωβον / ܘܠܝܥܩܘܒ / Jacobum; the Syriac binds conjunction, object-marker and name into one orthographic unit, against the Greek and Latin which separate the connective.
Ἰωάννην / ܘܠܝܘܚܢܢ / Joannem; as with James, the Peshitta agglutinates waw, the lamadh object-marker and the proper name into a single token.

The Clementine Vulgate inserts a colon after secum, dividing the verse into the act of taking the disciples and the onset of Jesus' distress; neither the Greek nor the Syriac mark this break lexically.
καὶ ἤρξατο / ܘܫܪܝ / et cœpit ('and he began'); all three render the ingressive 'began' governing the following infinitives, the Syriac ܘܫܪܝ again merging the conjunction.

Greek ἐκθαμβεῖσθαι ('to be greatly amazed/awe-struck') is rendered by Latin pavere ('to be terrified/dread') and Syriac ܠܡܬܟܡܪܘ (root k-m-r, 'to be saddened/downcast'); the three traditions emphasise different facets of distress, awe versus dread versus grief.
The coordinating conjunction καί / et linking the two infinitives; the Peshitta encodes it within the prefixed form of the following verb ܘܠܡܬܬܥܩܘ rather than as a separate token.

Greek ἀδημονεῖν ('to be deeply distressed/troubled') corresponds to Latin tædere ('to be weary/loathe') and Syriac ܘܠܡܬܬܥܩܘ ('to be in anguish/oppressed'); each version selects a cognate-distinct verb of inner turmoil, with the Latin tædere being the loosest equivalent.
